title: Glenn Martin Company employs Louis Witten for anti-gravity research
place_text: Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio; Johns Hopkins, Baltimore

tellings.quote: that word martin is coming all the way through was employing i believe lewis whitton edward whitton's father to do anti-gravity research somehow tied up with wright-patterson air force base in ohio and the johns hopkins university in baltimore maryland
Witten actually worked in Martin Corporation's Antigravity Research unit. That's right.
tellings.difference: Michels names the unit as Martin's RIAS antigravity research unit and states it firmly, while Weinstein hedges ("I believe") and links it to Wright-Patterson and Johns Hopkins.
tellings.link_reason: Both tellings say Louis Witten did anti-gravity research for the Martin company in the 1950s. Michels names the unit as RIAS, and Weinstein ties the work to Wright-Patterson and Johns Hopkins.

as_told.title: Louis Witten on his Wright Field gravity contract

plain: In the 1950s the aircraft maker Glenn Martin Company had a research unit, which Michels calls the Research Institute for Advanced Study, where the physicist Louis Witten, father of the physicist Edward Witten, worked on gravity, and some say anti-gravity, with ties to Wright Field, the Air Force base in Ohio later called Wright-Patterson. The mathematician Eric Weinstein brings it up with a hedge ("I believe"), adding Johns Hopkins University and names like the physicist Sheldon Glashow, while Michels states it flatly and links a Martin vice-president named George Trimble and the inventor Thomas Townsend Brown. Witten himself, in recorded interviews, says "the reason there was a laboratory at Wright Field was to find out what we were doing and to help us do it," and that he got a contract from them to study gravity, which he did "very happily," which would mean the military was quietly funding gravity research decades ago.
